channel.title: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
channel.description: Phys.org internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Expert comment: UK roads are dangerous by design. Punishing bad drivers won't fix them
item.description: In 2025, 1.16 million people around the world were killed in road collisions. That's 3,178 deaths per day. Up to 50 million were injured.

item.title: The art of success: Study shows arts education benefits students with disabilities
item.description: Give students with disabilities greater access to the arts, and good things happen: They come to school more often, face fewer disciplinary problems and improve their writing skills, according to new research from the University of Missouri.

item.title: Climate change and habitat loss could fuel deadly bat-borne disease
item.description: Bats carry some of the world's deadliest viruses. Now, as climate change, extreme heat and habitat destruction intensify, so too could the risk of these diseases spreading to humans, according to new Adelaide University research.

item.title: Prehistoric ecosystems could hold clues to preventing future wildfires
item.description: Could bringing back large herbivores help preserve Europe's rural landscapes and reduce wildfire risk? This is one of the key questions explored by an international study involving the University of Zaragoza, recently published in the journal Ecosystem Services.

item.title: Exquisite X-rays and dynamic compression initiate a new era of physics experiments on plutonium
item.description: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) and Washington State University (WSU) have conducted the first dynamic compression experiments on plutonium at a national light source facility, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS).

item.title: Policy changes in Canada had little effect on sales of antibiotics for animals, study finds
item.description: Sales of antibiotics for use in food-producing animals have fallen by 11% in Canada since 2018, but not because of federal policy changes.

item.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
item.description: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

item.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
item.description: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

item.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
item.description: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.

item.title: Should we save every old building?
item.description: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.

item.title: First lunar-specific ground motion model could guide seismic hazard assessments on moon
item.description: Civil engineers looking forward to building structures on the moon need to know how ground motion from moonquakes will affect these buildings. But will ground motion models developed for Earth work well for the lunar landscape?

item.title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below
item.description: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline.

item.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
item.description: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

item.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
item.description: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

item.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
item.description: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

item.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
item.description: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.

item.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
item.description: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

item.title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments
item.description: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it.

item.title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation
item.description: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.

item.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
item.description: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

item.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
item.description: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

item.title: Who's to blame for a rogue AI? New legal framework maps accountability
item.description: Cyberattacks and other harms caused by artificial intelligence challenge the ability of laws to determine who is liable. Product liability law would point to the company that built the AI model, but AIs are trained on data the company didn't produce, and the legions of people who have used them also played a role. Free speech and social media immunity laws that treat an AI agent as responsible for its own actions could imply the AI agent deserves the same rights as a person.

item.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
item.description: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

item.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
item.description: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

item.title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species
item.description: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.

item.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
item.description: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

item.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
item.description: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

item.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
item.description: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

item.title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal
item.description: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.

item.title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters
item.description: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.
